draft.title: Quantifiers
card: For all
A statement with "for all" (written ∀) claims that every member of a set fits. For example, "for all integers n, n² ≥ 0" claims it for every integer.
There exists
A statement with "there exists" (written ∃) claims that at least one member of a set fits. For example, "there exists an integer n with n² = 49" is true, because n = 7 works.
One member that fails is called a counterexample. A single counterexample shows that a "for all" statement is false.
Example: "for all integers n, n² > n" is false. Take n = 1: 1² = 1, and 1 is not greater than 1. To show a "there exists" statement is true, one member that fits is enough.
draft.remember: For all needs every case to work. There exists needs just one case to work.

a.q: Which single value of n shows that "for all integers n, n + 3 > 5" is false?
a.why: For n = 2, n + 3 = 5, and 5 is not greater than 5, so the claim fails. The values 4, 10 and 100 all give results above 5, so they fit the statement and cannot disprove it.
a.clue: Find a value where n + 3 is not above 5.

b.q: Which statement about the integers is true?
opts: There exists an integer n with n + 4 = 1
There exists an integer n with n² = −4
For all integers n, n² > n
b.why: With n = −3, n + 4 = 1, so one integer fits and the "there exists" statement is true. The second fails at n = −5, which gives −1. The third fails because no integer squared is negative. The fourth fails at n = 0, since 0 is not greater than 0.
b.clue: For a "for all" statement, test one value that might fail it.

b.best: There exists an integer n with n + 4 = 1

problems.detail: The why names the wrong options by position. In the order shown, the second option is 'for all n, n² > n' (fails at n = 0) and the fourth is 'there exists n with n² = −4' (no integer squared is negative). The why pairs 'second' with n = −5 and 'fourth' with n = 0, so it does not match the options students see. Refer to each option by its wording, not its position.

final.title: Quantifiers
card: For all
A statement with "for all" (written ∀) claims that every member of a set fits. For example, "for all integers \(n\), \(n^{2} \ge 0\)" is true, because no integer squared is negative.
There exists
A statement with "there exists" (written ∃) claims that at least one member of a set fits. For example, "there exists an integer \(n\) with \(n^{2} = 49\)" is true, because \(n = 7\) works.
One member that fails is called a counterexample. A single counterexample shows that a "for all" statement is false.
Example: "for all integers \(n\), \(n^{2} > n\)" is false. Take \(n = 1\): \(1^{2} = 1\), and 1 is not greater than 1. To show a "there exists" statement is true, one member that fits is enough.
final.remember: For all needs every case to work. There exists needs just one case to work.

a.q: Which single value of \(n\) shows that "for all integers \(n\), \(n + 3 > 5\)" is false?
a.why: For \(n = 2\), \(n + 3 = 5\), and 5 is not greater than 5, so the claim fails. The values 4, 10 and 100 all give results above 5, so they fit the statement and cannot disprove it.
a.clue: Find a value where \(n + 3\) is not above 5.

b.q: Which statement about the integers is true?
b.why: With \(n = -3\), \(n + 4 = 1\), so one integer fits and the "there exists" statement is true. The claim "for all integers \(n\), \(n + 4 > 1\)" fails at \(n = -5\), which gives \(-1\), and "for all integers \(n\), \(n^{2} > n\)" fails at \(n = 0\), since 0 is not greater than 0. No integer squared is negative, so no integer has \(n^{2} = -4\).
b.clue: For a "for all" statement, test one value that might fail it.
